title.narrative: Renewable Energy For Refugees, Phase II (RE4R Phase II)

description.narrative: Insatsen har som målsättning att öka tillgången och användingen av energi för utsatta människor i och utanför Rwandas fem flyktingläger. Med en marknadsansats kommer Practical Action öka tillgången till rena matlagningsmetoder, gatubelysning och förnybara ellösningar för hemmen. Under insatsen kommer också mindre företag få företagsutbildning och delfinansiering för energilösningar kopplade till deras företagsideer. Företagen kommer också ha tillgång till nya eller omgjorda företagscenter inom och utanför flyktinglägret. Insatsen har ett uttalat och välutvecklat jämställdhets fokus. Förändringar i matlagningsmetoder har i Rwanda en nära koppling till anpassningsåtgärder då avskogning i det bergiga landskapet är ett stort problem och leder till erosion.

The contribution aims to increase access to energy in Rwanda´s five refugee camps and their host communities. Practical action will use a market-based approach to increase access to clean cooking solutions, streetlights and renewable energy solutions in the homes. Small business will be supported with coaching and subsidies for their energy linked investments that are key to support their business models. Business will also have increased access to business centres in and outside of the camps. The contribution has a developed gender focus. In Rwanda, changing cooking methods are closely linked to efforts to avoid deforestation which in turn is an important adaptation measure as deforestation in combination with increased rainfalls leads to challenging erosion in the very hilly country.

The project is set to impact Rwanda's commitments to the Global Refugee Compact for Energy and Infrastructure and support achievement of SDG 7 for last mile communities. And the following outcomes and targets will support the achievement:
Outcome 1. Refugee communities in all camps in Rwanda and the surrounding host communities have access to affordable, low-carbon and environmentally friendly energy for household, business and community uses. By the end of the project there should be a 70% camp-wide uptake of minimum tier 1 renewable energy solutions for electricity. With regards to electricity for SME's, 300 enterprises should be reached through the Productive use of Energy (PUE) for livelihoods program. Furthermore, 80% of the total area of refugee camps is to be covered by public lighting and a number of renewable energy solution for institutions/community buildings in and around camps.
Outcome 2. Refugees in all camps and the surrounding host communities benefit from improved quality of life and livelihoods through strengthened markets and increased economic activity. 70% of households of target population self-report improved quality of life as a result of the project and 70% of supported PUE business report a 50% increase to their business income. Also, a total of 200 dignified jobs to be secured in refugee and host communities.
Outcome 3. Humanitarian stakeholders in Rwanda and in the wider, global humanitarian sector priorities renewable energy solutions, endorse, adopt and replicate Practical Action´s approach, and include refugee energy and livelihoods needs in their plans and policies at local, national and international levels 10 target stakeholders report they have planned or committed to adopt approaches promoted through the project 5 strategic practices at local, national, and international (including policies, response plans and project designs) have been informed or adapted to improve energy access for refugees and host communities as a result of the project.

sector.narrative: Energy generation, renewable sources - multiple technologies

description.narrative:
Intervention: Solar home systems (SHS) planned target: 7 047 Solar Home systems
Practical Action has contracted two private partners, Solektra and Belecom to deliver Solar home systems (SHS) and aftersales services in the camps and the host communities. Each company has implemented Solar Home Systems (SHS) throughout the five refugee camps. Last years numbers are reported in the brackets. As of now, 4 666 (1 980) SHS units have been sold and installed, with Solektra accounting for 3 250 (780) installations and Belecom for 1 416 (1,200). Companies have suffered from increased foreign exchange rates and high inflation in the country. Solectra has reached its target on delivery and installation. Belgacom are still delayed. During the year 3, 24/25, it was agreed to allow Practical Action to increase the prices by using the currency exchange rate gain (with conditions). Evening activities: Refugees can now effectively perform tasks such as cooking, household chores, and business operations after dark. According to the survey, 90% of respondents reported being able to engage in recreational activities after dark, reflecting enhanced access to leisure and improved quality of life during evening hours. Education support: Students benefit greatly, as the lighting allows for nighttime study and revision. According to the outcome monitoring survey, 84% of respondents reported that they are now able to study effectively after dark, highlighting a significant improvement in their learning environment and access to educational opportunities. Safety and security improvement: According to the outcome monitoring survey, 98% of refugees feel safer in homes after dark. Refugees have also indicated that improved lighting enables them to perform household chores and make social visits at night. These lighting interventions have significantly promoted both socialization and security within the camps. The SHS connections are made to a small majority of female led households (54%).
Intervention: Clean cooking planned target: 9 400 cook stoves and fuels
Practical Action has contracts with three private partners: Ecogreen, MC Green, and Agroplast. These partners are responsible for distributing cook stoves and pellets within the camp and the host community across all five refugee camps. As of now, with last year numbers in brackets: the companies have collectively sold 3 965 stoves (2,649) and 398 076 Kg of pellets (294,800). Ecogreen has sold 1 172 stoves (1,059) stoves and 195 144 kg of pellets (146 060), MC Green has sold 2 453 stoves (1,579) and 201 926 kg of pellets (148,740), while Agroplast has sold a total of 340 stoves (11) and 1 006 kg of pellets (0). The results are clearly still below the targeted 9 400 cook stoves that was planned. Companies are facing challenges regarding the pricing due to foreign exchange rate and inflation in Rwanda the past two years. There are also challenges related between the so called forced and natural air draft versions of the stoves where refugees naturally prefer the forced air draft stoves as they are more fuel efficient and include a small solar device that can be used for instance to charge a mobile. However, companies production capacities are challenged to meet the demand of forced air draft stoves. The forced air draft stoves are also significantly more expensive. The outcome monitoring survey done in june 2024, 63% percent of respondents reported that adopting clean cooking technologies has significantly enhanced safety and health within their homes. Additionally, 78% percent expressed satisfaction with the quality of the improved cookstoves, underscoring the meaningful impact these innovations have had on their daily lives. "The stove can be purchased through convenient instalment options. It significantly reduces cooking time compared to traditional methods, improves overall hygiene, and effectively retains heat, keeping meals warm throughout the dayeven when left on the stove in the morning," shared Judith and Olive from Nyabiheke refugee camp.
Intervention: Institutional/Solar street lights, planned target: 815 street lights installed
Practical Action has signed a contract with Solektra Rwanda Limited for the supply and installation of solar streetlights across five refugee camps. The installation of 815 solar streetlights is complete and has greatly improved community life, facilitating social interactions, leisure activities, and mobility. According to the outcome monitoring survey, ninety seven percent of respondents indicated that the installation of street lighting has consistently enhanced their night time activities outside the home, such as work and community events. Furthermore, 95 percent reported a notable improvement in overall community safety because of the powered solar streetlights. Additional funding was recived from Practical Action main office to install an additional 17 street lights in Mahama. These were especially used to connect the newly constructed business center (outside of the camp) with the camp.
Intervention: Business centers and business supported
To efficiently utilize energy, 300 entrepreneurs have been recruited and are receiving support. All 300 receive basic business support including making a work plan. Depending on their needs, they benefit from more in-depth business support, some are offered a co-investment in equipment or outside training in cooperation with others. The construction of business centers in Kiziba, Mugombwa and in Kirehe (outside of the Mahama camp) is completed. The business center in Mugombwa hosts 50 entrepreneurs, Kiziba 40 entrepreneurs and Mahama that that was inaugurated January 2025, hosts 150 entrepreneurs and a (very) small day care facility. The mentoring program focuses on key areas such as recordkeeping, marketing, capital raising for business expansion, and the procurement of productive use of energy (PUE) appliances. This has for example led to: 300 entrepreneurs have access to electricity to power their businesses, providing essential lighting and the ability to operate small appliances, and 120 of them have received financing to acquire appliances to enable their business work plans. 74% of the supported entrepreneurs have increased their sales with 30% or more. Out of them, 44% of the supported entrepreneurs have increased their sales with 50% or more. 24 new market linkages were established hence, facilitating access to new markets for entrepreneurs. Businesses that were facilitated to access new markets include, tailoring, canteen, butcher, dairy, poultry through egg incubation, and milling. 11 entrepreneurs graduated and hence opened new outlets within the host community due to increased profit from their businesses, mentorship training is still provided to these businesses. 15 entrepreneurs were linked to other institutions to receive vocational training on how to operate PUE appliances. This was facilitated through partnerships with organizations such as World Vision and Maison Shalom. Established partnerships with prominent livelihood partners such as Caritas, GIZ, Inkomoko, and Umutanguha. These collaborations are centered on improving access to financial services and providing vocational training opportunities to PUE entrepreneurs.
Below are some collected voices from the refugee community:
- Claude operates a butcher in the Kiziba Refugee Camp supplying meat, meat pies and filled pastries to local restaurants in Kizba Refugee camps. In sept 2024, RE4R II helped Claude to access capital in order to procure a meat freezer, whilst also offering business management training in areas such as recording keeping, customer care, marketing, appliance maintenance, and health and safety standards. Claude says that this support marked a turning point for his business: "I have created 3 jobs and my monthly profit has increased from $80 to $ 200 - Macozi: Women's Dairy Family Kiziba (PUE): "With our dairy business, we make a profit of 300$ per month and have created 3 jobs for refugees. Thanks to the monthly profit from our dairy business, we have now expanded our business to cheese making, which will support our aim of tripling our monthly profit". - Elie in Kiziba: "This business center has helped my photography business in many ways. It has enabled me to have a studio where people of all ages in the camp come to create memories. It has allowed me to expand the business to also include services such as Irembo and software, a photocopy and printing machine. The majority of the branding of the businesses in the center was designed and printed by me. With a monthly profit of $150, I am also providing photography training to 10 young people in the camp."
Gender working groups: The creation of Gender Working Groups in five refugee camps, consisting of a total 41 women and 34 men, aims to foster dialogue and collaboration towards gender equity and inclusion. This initiative also enables both women and men to engage with renewable energy solutions, bolstering confidence and enhancing awareness about gender transformation and inclusion in the energy sector. Under the productive use of energy (PUE) intervention, through peer-to-peer leanings, women entrepreneurs are connected with champions to enhance their business skills. Some Gender Working Group members are among PUE entrepreneurs (see example above). Gender Working Group members share their experiences during monthly meetings, demonstrating various income generating activities made possible through energy access. As a result, three savings groups have been established by the members.
